Basal metabolic rate measurements in Geomys pinetis, obtained from respirometry trials conducted under controlled laboratory conditions, reveal a maximum oxygen consumption of 142 milliliters per hour [JOi = 142 milliliters per hour] when the animals were maintained at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This value, reflective of the species' fossorial lifestyle and low resting metabolism, is consistent with expectations for a small-bodied subterranean rodent that must economize energy expenditure within the thermally stable yet oxygen-limited burrow environment. The particular temperature at which this maximum rate was recorded corresponds to the species' normothermic core body temperature during periods of inactivity, a state that minimizes overall energy demands.

Female Southeastern pocket gophers attain a maximum adult body mass of 136 grams [Wwi = 136 grams], whereas conspecific males reach a substantially higher ultimate wet weight of 176 grams [Wwi = 176 grams], a pattern of sexual size dimorphism commonly observed across pocket gopher species. This divergence in mass likely reflects differential selective pressures associated with territorial defense in males and the energetic constraints of gestation and lactation in females. Neonates of this species are altricial at birth, with a recorded wet weight of 5.2 grams [Wwb = 5.2 grams] based on data extrapolated from the closely related plains pocket gopher, Geomys bursarius. This small birth mass is typical among geomyids and is associated with a relatively short gestation period and highly dependent early development within the maternal burrow system.

Reproductive output in Geomys pinetis is characterized by small litter sizes, typically ranging from one to three pups per litter [N_R_i = one to three pups per litter], with breeding females capable of producing up to three litters each year [F_R_i = up to three litters each year] under favorable environmental conditions at a burrow temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This annual reproductive strategy, combining modest litter sizes with multiple potential litters, represents a relatively conservative approach typical of subterranean rodents that face high metabolic costs associated with digging and limited above-ground foraging opportunities. The interval between successive litters can be quite short, allowing females to sustain high annual fecundity when resource availability permits continuous breeding throughout much of the year.

Gestation in the Southeastern pocket gopher spans approximately 45 days [tg = approximately 45 days] when measured at a maternal body temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], with reported durations from field and captive studies falling within a range of 40 to 50 days. Following parturition, the altricial pups remain entirely dependent on maternal care and milk provisioning for a period of about 30 days [tx = about 30 days] before they are weaned, an interval also recorded at the typical burrow temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. Weaning marks the onset of nutritional independence, after which the young must begin excavating their own tunnel systems and foraging for roots and tubers, a challenging transition that imposes high juvenile mortality in this species.

Sexual maturation in Geomys pinetis occurs relatively early, with individuals reaching puberty at approximately 120 days after birth [tp = approximately 120 days after birth] under the stable thermal conditions of the natal burrow at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This rapid developmental trajectory allows young of the year to potentially breed during their first spring if born early in the preceding reproductive season. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species is approximately 2 years [am = approximately 2 years] at a burrow temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], a relatively short duration that underscores the high mortality risks faced by small fossorial mammals in the wild, including predation from snakes, raptors, and carnivorous mammals, as well as the physiological challenges of their subterranean existence.
